newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solana in renewed bid to defuse Greek-Turkish row.
newsitem.headline: Solana in renewed bid to defuse Greek-Turkish row.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana leaves on Wednesday for a two-day official visit to Turkey in a fresh attempt to reduce tensions with fellow NATO member Greece in the eastern Mediterranean.

Solana, who also visited both countries last year, will urge Ankara to agree a number of confidence-building measures to avoid the danger of any armed clashes between the two who almost came to blows last year over a disputed uninhabited rocky islet.
"Solana will be emphasising he has a mandate to lower the temperature between the two," said one NATO official, adding Solana would visit Athens towards the end of the month.

His main task is to get the two sides to agree to have independent monitors on each other's ships, set up a telephone 'hotline' between the two capitals, and make more use of information garnered from alliance surveillance aircraft.

Solana's trip comes at a time of renewed tension over Cyprus which has announced plans to base Russian anti-aircraft missiles on its territory in response to overflights of the Greek Cypriot part of the island by Turkish war planes.

NATO officials fear the continuing crisis in relations between two key members on its strategic southern flank could spill over into plans to reform the alliance and take in new members from former communist Europe.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, also deputy prime minister in the Islamist-led government, has warned the West Ankara could veto NATO's eastwards expansion if its aspirations for closer ties with the European Union remain frustrated.
Turkey signed a customs union with the EU last year, but Greece has blocked much of the aid expected to flow to Ankara under the deal.

Ciller and other secular pro-western politicians in Turkey fear they will lose out further to the Islamists, who formed modern Turkey's first non-secular government last year, unless they can deliver on promised close ties with the West.
Europe's "big five" powers told Turkey last week it had every right to aspire to full EU membership, but first must make progress on human rights, the Kurdish issue and its disputes with Greece.
Foreign ministers from Britain, France, Germany, Spain and Italy urged Ciller not to block NATO expansion and continue to look to Europe rather than shift towards its Moslem neighbours.
European capitals are increasingly concerned about the noises coming out of Ankara since Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan took power.

"We're always hearing statements we don't like... I am going to take it seriously because we have known that this is possible," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country is the current EU presidency, said on Wednesday.
Speaking to the European Parliament, van Mierlo said it was time for some plain speaking with regard to Turkey's hopes.
"There is a problem of a large Moslem state. Do we want that in Europe? It is an unspoken question," van Mierlo said.

Turkey signed an association agreement with what is now the European Union as long ago as 1963. It formally applied to join the bloc in 1987 and has watched with mounting anger as former communist countries moved ahead in the queue.
Formal negotiations with as many as 11 countries from central and eastern Europe are due to start around the end of this year.
Ankara is also blocking progress on a landmark deal to allow the Western European Union (WEU), the EU's nascent defence arm, to use NATO equipment for European-only missions.
Turkey only has observer status at the WEU which does not permit it to take part in planning for such operations.
"Solana will stress the need to keep NATO, WEU and EU politics apart," said the official.
